It's a pretty crazy situation and I've been following pretty closely, will try and break it down how I see it as best I can:

First issue is the legality of the referendum, and its relevance to self-determination. The vote was illegal. There were numerous procedural improprieties in the way that the referendum was organized. The Catalonian Parliament didn't follow all of the proper procedures in voting to hold the referendum, and that causes it to be suspect. I don't agree with the Spanish claim that their Constitution can forbid independence and needs to be amended, but there are still issues with the way the vote was held. However, because the issues were merely procedural, it doesn't seem like the vote would have been avoided had they been followed. At the same time, its hard to call the referendum legitimate when the procedures weren't followed. So you have both sides with their heels dug in claiming the referendum was either legal or illegal, and it seems impossible that either will change their mind. This means that the Spanish can continue to claim that the referendum was illegal, and the Catalonians can keep claiming it was legitimate and there really never will be any resolution on that question. Since the Spanish government's claims to illegitimacy rest on the constitution that won't be changed, and not the shenanigans in Parliament, there's zero room for compromise. What this means is that there really is no right answer to the legality of the referendum, and no possibility for one to emerge through reasonable negotiation.

The next point I think is important is that this isn't really a movement about securing the independence of Catalonian people and culture, and the vote isn't about a homogeneous region uniting around their shared heritage. It is purely economic, as Catalonia ships more money to Madrid than they get back relative to other regions. They also have less autonomy than the Basque country, who have more control over their taxation than Catalonia. This of course doesn't make independence illegitimate but its certainly important to remember in the context of an ongoing negotiation. It is a small percentage of people who are strongly in favor of independence, maybe 10-15%, and a small percentage adamantly opposed, another 5-15%. The people in the middle seem to be much more moderate as you'd expect, taking a view that the current situation needs to be changed, but that reconciliation is possible, if Spain is willing to make concessions. Spain, however, has taken a hard line and basically offered no concessions that they're willing to live up to. This means that the 70% in the middle are split between those who still want to negotiate and those who think that Spain has failed to offer anything meaningful and therefore secession is the only option left, or that voting for independence will at least but Catalonia in a better negotiating position.

The next major issue is that the anti-independence walked out of the Parliament in response to the way that the vote to hold the referendum went down, and then the same groups discouraged their people from voting at all in the Referendum because they claimed it was illegitimate. Storming off in protest seems dramatic and may be effective in some contexts, but here the result has been that the referendum went forward, and the vote totals reflect that the "no" voters didn't show up, leaving them with about 10% of the vote based on only 40% turnout. We therefore have no real idea how to extrapolate that result to the general public as "no" voters have a reasonable claim that they shouldn't be disenfranchised for their non-participation in an illegal referendum.

As far as how this should be viewed from the perspective of individual liberty, and the future of the EU and Spain, I've heard mixed opinions. Some make the argument that self-determination is integral to any notion of individual liberty, while others argue that an independent Catalonia will likely embrace full-on socialism and go as hard left as any nation in Europe, and therefore will be detrimental to the cause of individual liberty. Unfortunately, both are probably correct, and the revolution is therefore neither a total win or total loss for either side.

Sorry if this raises more questions than it answers, but this situation will be playing out for awhile and I'm not sure there really is a good answer. Neither side wants to negotiate at this point, the conflict has turned violent, and neither side can be said to be unambiguously right or wrong. My only hope is that the violence can end and that the situation can be peacefully resolved.

Communications aren't perfect, on-site eyewitness accounts conflict, and people calling in with part of the picture may feel absolutely certain they know what is going on when they patently don't.

In this scenario, I think what happened is dispatch got flooded with both 911 calls and cops calling in saying "ACTIVE SHOOTER at my location!". Which was completely true if they happened to be on the ground anywhere in the area where bullets were raining down.

The fact that the actual shooter(s) was 350 or 500 yards away was irrelevant to those under fire. Same with people calling in from Mandalay or Tropicana or wherever: "I hear massive amounts of gunfire!".

Cops and dispatchers have to filter all that in real-time, and in the case of a large event like this there's an absolutely massive amount of comms traffic. Inevitably there is a lot of misinformation and bad/useless calls. That's not a conspiracy, just "the fog of war".
